fixes.explanation: I get why you'd hope so, friend, but the text says otherwise. “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” Jeroboam was king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Throughout their days is how the text puts it.

Yes, baker. The text says, “There was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam throughout their days.” Jeroboam was the king of Israel, the northern kingdom. Two kings, and war between them throughout their days.

That's the one, baker. Rehoboam, Solomon's son, is king in Judah, and the text says their sins “…provoked Him to jealous anger more than all their fathers had done.” That's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be.

I see why that one tempts you, baker, but the text says the opposite. Under King Rehoboam, Judah's worship didn't look nothing like those nations. The text says, “They imitated all the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.” Imitating them is the opposite of looking nothing like them.

That's right, baker. The text says Judah, under King Rehoboam, “…imitated all the abominations of the nations the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.” Judah copied what those nations had done. It's a sobering verse, and the text doesn't soften it.

Not this one, baker. The text names what Shishak, Egypt's king, seized: the treasures of the house of the LORD and of the royal palace. It says “He took everything, including all the gold shields that Solomon had made.” The captives answer isn't what the text gives.
Bronze it is, baker. Shishak, Egypt's king, had taken the gold shields Solomon had made, so Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place. Same job, less shine. Gold to bronze is a rough trade.
Gold is what the old shields were made of, friend. Shishak, Egypt's king, took all the gold shields that Solomon, Rehoboam's father, had made. Then King Rehoboam made bronze ones in their place.

Right, baker. The text says Rehoboam rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the City of David. Rehoboam is Solomon's son, as the text says when it introduces him. The City of David is the place the text names.

Nice hope, friend, but that's not what the text says. Abijam, Rehoboam's son, “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…” The text adds that “…his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God as the heart of David his forefather had been.”

That's more like what Abijam's son Asa does, baker. Asa removed all the idols that his fathers had made. Abijam, Rehoboam's son, went the other direction, since the text says he “…walked in all the sins that his father before him had committed…”

Abraham is a big name, friend, and I've grabbed the biggest name in the room before myself. The writer sets Abijam beside David instead. The text says his heart was not as fully devoted to the LORD his God “…as the heart of David his forefather had been.”

That's it. The text says the LORD gave Abijam a lamp in Jerusalem “…by raising up a son to succeed him and to make Jerusalem strong.” The lamp is a son, and Asa is that son. The text says the LORD did it for the sake of David.

Plenty of people would've let it slide, friend, but Asa didn't. He removed his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole. Then Asa chopped down the pole and burned it in the Kidron Valley.

That's it, baker. The text says that although the high places were not removed, “…Asa’s heart was fully devoted to the LORD all his days.” The writer says it plainly and doesn't hedge. Abijam's heart, by contrast, was not as fully devoted as the heart of David.
Yes, baker. Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah “…to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah.” The text pairs leaving with entering. Entering is the word.

Defending sounds close, baker, but that's not the word. Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. The word in the verse is entering.

Taxing is a fun guess, friend, and I'd be braced for a toll booth too. But the text says Baasha, king of Israel, fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah. No toll in the verse, just those two words.

Right, baker. Asa sent his servants with the silver and gold to Ben-hadad, king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus. Asa was asking a foreign king for help. The silver and gold went along with a message.

Yes, baker. Asa's message says, “Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me.” The silver and gold were a gift sent along with that request. The whole ask is in that one line.

That's a sensible idea, friend, but Asa didn't ask for it. His message asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that Baasha would withdraw from him. Guarding Jerusalem isn't in the message.

Peace would've been something, baker, but that's not the request. Asa asked Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that Baasha would withdraw from him. Making peace isn't in that message.
That's not how it went, baker. The text says Ben-hadad “…listened to King Asa…” and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. Staying loyal to Baasha isn't what the text shows.

Right, baker. The text says Ben-hadad “…listened to King Asa…” and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel. That's the opposite of staying loyal to Baasha. He conquered Ijon, Dan, Abel-beth-maacah, and the whole land of Naphtali.

Yes, baker. The text says, “When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.” He stopped as soon as he learned of it. By then, Ben-hadad's commanders were conquering cities of Israel.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and withdrew to Tirzah.” He stopped, and he withdrew. Then King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah.

That's it, baker. King Asa summoned all the men of Judah, with no exceptions, and they “…carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building.” Stones and timbers, all hauled off. With no exceptions is how the text puts it.

Finishing sounds like the natural next step, friend, but that's not what the men of Judah did. They carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. Carrying them off is the opposite of finishing.

Yes, baker. With those materials, King Asa built up Geba of Benjamin, as well as Mizpah. The materials were the stones and timbers Baasha had used for building. Those same stones and timbers went to work on Geba and Mizpah.
That's not what the text says, baker. Asa had a long reign of forty-one years, but the text says, “In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet.” So he wasn't healthy right to the end.
That's right, baker. The text says, “In his old age, however, he became diseased in his feet.” I think that's a hard note to end on, and the text just states it.
Jehoram isn't the name in this verse, baker. The text says Asa rested with his fathers and was buried with them in the city of his father David. Then his son Jehoshaphat reigned in his place.
